title: Thermal stress by chaining Steps
summary: Feed a heat Step's solved temperature field straight into a static Step's load with step.add.after, check the result against a closed form, and catch the one mistake that makes a symmetry constraint invent stress that was never there.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: A steel plate, conducted through and then read as a mechanical load. Two physics, one Model, and the point of this tutorial is the seam between them.

steps.title: Units
steps.explain: Metres, megapascals, and degrees Celsius for the temperature axis.

steps.title: Plane strain
steps.explain: A one-metre-square slab, thick enough in the missing third direction that it cannot contract through it: plane strain. That choice matters later — the closed form this tutorial checks against assumes it.

steps.title: Sketch the plate
steps.explain: A plain square, one edge per tag: `ymin`, `xmax`, `ymax`, `xmin`.

steps.title: Material, with alpha and k both
steps.explain: This Material is used by two different Steps for two different properties: `k` for the heat Step's conduction, `E`, `nu` and `alpha` for the static Steps' thermal stress. One Material, both physics — nothing about `material.add` knows a chained analysis is coming.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: One Material, one Body.

steps.title: Mesh it
steps.explain: A 10 × 10 lattice at `order: 2` — plenty for a field that varies linearly in one direction.

steps.title: Cold at the bottom
steps.explain: `constraint.temperature` — the same Dirichlet boundary the `heat-conduction` tutorial used. Held at 0 °C.

steps.title: Hot at the top
steps.explain: 100 °C at the other edge, so the plate carries a temperature field that runs linearly from 0 to 100 °C bottom to top — a real gradient, not a single number.

steps.title: The heat Step
steps.explain: `procedure: "heat-steady"`, no mechanical Loads at all — this Step's entire job is to produce a temperature field, not a stress. It is not solved yet; a chained Step needs its own definitions in place first, so every Step in this Model gets built before any of them gets solved. (Solving `conduct` now and adding more Commands afterward would make its Result stale the moment anything downstream changed the Model — try it and the engine will say so.)

steps.title: A point to pin
steps.explain: One node at the origin, named so a constraint can target just it rather than a whole edge.

steps.title: One real wall
steps.explain: Suppose this plate is cast against a fixed wall on its left edge and free everywhere else in x — a slab poured against one foundation, open to the air on the other side. `dofs: ["ux"]` restrains only the x-displacement, leaving the plate free to bow or slide in y.

steps.title: Pin the rigid-body freedom
steps.explain: One edge fixed in x already stops x-translation and in-plane rotation; the plate can still slide as a whole in y. One point, fixed in `uy` only, removes that last freedom without resisting any real deformation anywhere else.

steps.title: The Load that isn't a Load
steps.explain: `load.temperature` with `value` equal to `reference` looks like it does nothing — it doesn't set a temperature at all. What it actually does is tell a chained static Step to read thermal strain from the Step it chains to rather than from a constant: this is the half of `step.add{after}` that lives on the Load side.

steps.title: Chain it: the wall, and nothing else
steps.explain: `after: "conduct"` is the whole trick. This static Step does not repeat the temperature boundary conditions — once solved, it will read `conduct`'s field directly, node by node, as the thermal load. With only the one real wall in the constraint list, the right edge is left completely free.

steps.title: The trap: a symmetry constraint on a free edge
steps.explain: Now suppose, out of habit, you also constrain the right edge in a second version of the stress Step — not because there is a wall there (there isn't), but because `constraint.symmetry` "only removes the normal displacement" and feels harmless, or because a square plate looks like it ought to be symmetric. It is not: nothing about this temperature field or this geometry is symmetric about x = 1, which is an *edge*, not a mirror plane. This Set does not touch `stress-free` at all — it exists only for the Step defined next.

steps.title: Chain it again, with the extra constraint
steps.explain: Same heat field, same real wall, plus the symmetry constraint that was never justified.

steps.title: Now make the second wall real
steps.explain: Suppose instead the plate genuinely is cast between two fixed abutments, restrained in x at both edges for a real, physical reason. `constraint.fix` says exactly that, and says it honestly — no symmetry argument required, because there is nothing to be symmetric about: both edges are simply walls.

steps.title: Chain it a third time: the real, checked model
steps.explain: Both walls, the one pin, the chained thermal load — this is the model `docs/EXAMPLES.md` and `BENCHMARKS.md` both check. Three static Steps now sit on this Model, all chained to `conduct`, all still unsolved.

steps.title: Solve the heat Step first
steps.explain: Every Command that touches this Model is now in place, so solving can finally start — `conduct` first, since the other three all read its Result.

steps.title: Solve the free plate: no stress
steps.explain: σₓₓ at mid-height comes out at machine-zero. Nothing is stopping the plate from expanding into the temperature field it was just given, so it does — and free thermal expansion, however large, carries no stress at all. Only a restraint converts expansion into stress; there is only one restraint here, and it does not resist x.

steps.title: Solve the trap: −150 MPa, and it is fake
steps.explain: σₓₓ at mid-height is now −150 MPa — the same number the fully-restrained plate below is about to compute, because a symmetry constraint zeroing ux at x = 1 restrains the plate's x-expansion exactly as a second wall would. But there is no second wall in this version of the model: the −150 MPa here is an artefact of a restraint that has no physical counterpart, not a measurement of anything the real, one-walled plate would do. The number cannot tell you which case you are in; only knowing what you actually built can.

steps.title: Solve the real model: the same number, for real this time
steps.explain: σₓₓ at mid-height is −150 MPa again — identical to the trap, digit for digit. The physics that makes it real this time is that both walls actually exist; nothing about the number itself changed, or could have.

steps.title: The closed form, and which is which
steps.explain: One formula, and the reminder that a stress number is only as trustworthy as the restraint that produced it.
steps.theory:
For a plate held against x-displacement at both edges, free in y, under a temperature change $\Delta T$ from its stress-free reference (plane strain, so $\varepsilon_{zz}=0$ too): $\varepsilon_{xx}=0$ and $\sigma_{yy}=0$ give
$$\sigma_{xx} = \sigma_{zz} = -\frac{E\,\alpha\,\Delta T}{1-\nu}.$$
At mid-height, $\Delta T = 50\,\mathrm{K}$, $E = 210\,\mathrm{GPa}$, $\alpha = 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $\nu = 0.3$: $\sigma_{xx} = -150\,\mathrm{MPa}$ exactly, and the mesh above computes it to $-0.00\,\%$ error.

**`step.add{after}`** is what makes this a *chained* thermal-stress analysis rather than a static Step with a hand-typed `load.temperature` value: the static Step reads `conduct`'s solved nodal temperatures directly, so the stress is linear in $y$ exactly as the real temperature field is, rather than uniform because someone typed one representative number. It also has a bookkeeping cost worth knowing: a chained Step needs the Step it names to have a Result that matches the *current* Model, hash for hash — so the practical order is always build everything, then solve, rather than interleaving the two, or an edit made after an early solve will stale it before a later chained Step can use it.

**Which is which.** Both `stress-wrong` and `stress` computed $-150\,\mathrm{MPa}$ at mid-height, and nothing in that number distinguishes them. The difference is entirely in what each restraint claims to be: `left` and `right` in `stress` are two walls that are genuinely there, so $-150\,\mathrm{MPa}$ is the plate's real answer to real end conditions. `wrongsym` in `stress-wrong` is a symmetry constraint invented for an edge with no wall and no mirror plane behind it, so its $-150\,\mathrm{MPa}$ is an artefact of that invented restraint — a measurement of the constraint, not of the plate. `stress-free`, with the same heat field and only the one real wall, is the tell: it computes zero, because a genuinely free thermal expansion carries no stress at all. Whenever a thermal-stress result looks suspiciously clean, or suspiciously large, the question is never "is the number right" — a correct solve of the wrong boundary conditions is still a correct solve — it is "does every restraint in the constraint list correspond to something that is actually there."
